Śunaśśepha
------------------------------------------
Śunaśśepha is a classic example to show that poverty and famine can drive even pious parents to sell their children.
He was the second son of Ajīgarta, a sage of the भृगु race. During a severe famine, unable to sustain his family, he sold शुनश्शेफ to the king हरिश्चन्द्र who was in search of a boy to be offered in a sacrifice he was performing. However, the great sage विश्वामित्र managed to save his life and adopted him as his own son, giving a new name, Devarāta.
Ajīgarta was reborn as a पिशाच (goblin) because of his sin. Devarāta however, redeemed him by the power of his austerities.
Śunaśśepha is the ṛṣi (the sage, the seer) of some Ṛgvedic mantras (1.2

). The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (Chapter 33) describes his story in great detail.
The story of शुनश्शेफ appears in the Rāmāyaṇa also (Bālakaṇḍa Chapters 61, 62). There, it is the king अम्बरीष and not Hairścandra, who purchased the boy. The sage विश्वामित्र who was the boy’s maternal uncle, taught him some secret mantras to please the god वरुण, by whose grace he was ultimately saved.

Sundarakāṇḍa
------------------------------------------
This is the fifth book of वाल्मीकि’s Rāmāyaṇa.
See RĀMĀYAṆA for details.

Śunāsīrīya
(‘guide of plough’)
------------------------------------------
This is the last of the four वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् grouped under the cāturmāsyas. It is referred to even in the Ṛgveda (4.57.5 and 8).
The word Śunā-sīra may refer to any of the following deities: वायु and सूर्य; सूर्य and इन्द्र; इन्द्र and two forms of अग्नि.
Offering हविस् (special oblations) in this sacrifice is considered as very important. It consists of पुरोडाश (rice) cakes in twelve mud plates as also milk.
This sacrifice can be performed at any time during the year. There is no उत्तरवेदि (high alter erected in the east). The fire is not produced by araṇis.
Attaining wealth and success in life are the twin purposes of performing this sacrifice.
See also CĀTURMĀSYA.

Sundaramūrti
------------------------------------------
Out of the sixty-three Nāyanmārs (or नायनार्स्), the great Śaiva saints of Tamil Nadu, four are considered most important. सुन्दरमूर्ति is one of them. He lived in the eighth century A. D.
He was the son of Śaḍaiyanār and Iśaijñāniyār. He was born in a small town, Tirunāvalūr. He was given the name Nambi Ārūran. He however came to be known as सुन्दरमूर्ति.
In his young age, he was adopted by Narasiṅga Munaiyaraiyar, the local king. Under his loving care, the boy grew into a fine young man, well-educated and cultured.
Just at the time of his मर्रिअगे, Lord शिव came, disguised as an old ब्राह्मण and claimed that this youth was his slave as per the agreement between him and the grandfather of the youth. The मर्रिअगे was abandoned. सुन्दरमूर्ति got the vision of शिव himself in that ब्राह्मण and became his ardent devotee. He sang a wonderfully poetic and melodious song inspired by the Lord Himself.
He then started on a long पिल्ग्रिमगे of all the sacred places connected with शिव. He was blessed with many divine visions and spiritual experiences and also performed several miracles to help the needy persons.
He had two wives—Paravaiyār and Saṅgiliyār (supposed to be divine damsels born on earth)—both of whom were also great devotees of शिव and loyal to their husband.
He is said to have departed for the world of शिव in the शिव temple at a place called Tiruvañjaikkaḷam.
Sundaramūrti’s compositions are part of the Tevāram (part of the seven books of collection known as Tirumurai) and are sung in शिव temples even today in Tamil Nadu. Only a hundred songs are available now though he is said to have composed thousands.
